minimum_safe_summary: This empirical study investigated whether exposure to restorative environments could restore attentional capacity after mental fatigue. Across three experiments, participants performed a sustained attention task, viewed photographs of restorative nature scenes, nonrestorative urban scenes, or geometrical patterns, and then repeated the attention task. Key findings showed that only exposure to restorative environments significantly improved attentional performance (increased D-prime and correct responses, decreased reaction times). Nonrestorative and geometrical pattern exposures did not yield similar benefits. While self-paced viewing of restorative scenes was longer, it did not lead to greater performance improvements than standardized viewing. The study's limitations include the relatively short exposure times, which may not have allowed for full restoration, and the need for future research to determine optimal exposure conditions.
